lessons.title: Engineering materials
lessons.summary: Steel, concrete, wood, aluminium and plastics.

cards.title: Strength and stiffness are different

items: steel stiff, aluminium a third as stiff

cards.text: Strength is how much stress a material takes before it breaks or yields. Stiffness is how much it resists bending or stretching. Rubber is weak and flexible; glass is stiff but brittle.

deep.x: Strength is how much stress a material withstands before failing. Stiffness is how much it resists deforming. A material can be strong but flexible, or stiff but weak.
Examples
Toughness
A third property, toughness, is the energy absorbed before fracture. Steel is tough; glass is not.
Design implications

x: Bridges must be stiff enough not to sway uncomfortably
Ropes must be strong but can stretch
Aircraft need strength and stiffness at low weight

deep.x: Strong, stiff and tough are three different virtues.

cards.title: Steel
cards.text: Steel is iron with a little carbon. It's strong in both tension and compression, ductile (bends before breaking) and recyclable, but heavy and rusts without protection.

deep.x: Steel is iron with a small amount of carbon, usually under 2%. It's the backbone of modern construction and machinery.
Grades
Recycling
Steel is one of the most recycled materials in the world. Electric arc furnaces melt scrap with much lower emissions than making new steel from ore.
Production
Steel's ductility gives warning before failure.

cards.title: Concrete
cards.text: Concrete is cement, water, sand and gravel. It's cheap and very strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel bars (rebar) are added where tension occurs.

deep.x: Concrete is a mix of cement, water, sand and gravel. It's the world's most used construction material after water.
Strength
Tensile strength is only about a tenth of compressive strength.
Curing
Concrete hardens through a chemical reaction with water, not by drying. It gains most of its strength in about 28 days and must be kept moist while curing.
Prestressed concrete
Steel tendons are tensioned before or after casting, squeezing the concrete so it stays in compression even under load. It allows longer spans.
Concrete loves compression; steel handles the tension.

cards.title: Wood
cards.text: Wood is strong along the grain and weak across it. For its weight it's remarkably strong, it stores carbon and is easy to work, but moisture, fire and insects must be managed.

deep.x: Wood is a natural composite of cellulose fibres in a lignin matrix. It's strong along the grain, light and renewable.
Strength for weight
Engineered timber
Modern timber buildings
Engineered timber now enables tall buildings: the Ascent tower in Milwaukee, completed in 2022, reaches about 87 m.
Challenges
Wood is a carbon store you can build with.

cards.title: Aluminium
cards.text: Aluminium is about a third the weight of steel and doesn't rust (a thin oxide layer protects it). It's less stiff, so parts are made thicker or shaped cleverly. Used in aircraft, window frames, cars.

deep.x: Aluminium is about a third the density of steel and naturally resists corrosion through a thin oxide layer.
Strengths and limits
Energy
Making new aluminium uses a lot of electricity. Recycling it uses about 5% of that energy, so recycled aluminium is highly valuable.
Uses
Light and corrosion-free, but less stiff than steel.

cards.title: Plastics and composites
cards.text: Plastics are light, cheap and mouldable. Composites like carbon fibre embed strong fibres in resin, giving very high strength and stiffness for their weight: bikes, aircraft, racing cars.

deep.x: Plastics are light, cheap and easy to shape. Composites combine materials to get properties neither has alone.

items.b: melt and reshape: PE, PP, PVC, nylon
very stiff and strong for weight

deep.x: Composites
Uses

items: Aircraft (e.g. Boeing 787 about 50% composites by weight)

deep.x: Drawbacks
Composites put strong fibres exactly where the loads go.

cards.title: Choosing a material
cards.text: Engineers weigh strength, stiffness, weight, cost, durability, ease of manufacture and environmental impact. There's never a perfect material, only the best compromise.

deep.x: Material selection balances many properties against cost and practicality. There's no perfect material, only the best compromise.
Ashby charts
Engineers use charts plotting properties against each other (like stiffness versus density) to find materials that best fit a requirement.
Example
Life-cycle thinking
The best material depends on what matters most for the job.

cards.title: Embodied carbon
cards.text: Making cement releases a lot of CO₂, about 8% of global emissions according to many estimates. Steel production is also carbon-heavy. That's driving interest in timber buildings and low-carbon cements.

deep.x: Embodied carbon is the greenhouse gas emitted in making materials and building structures. Cement and steel are major sources.

items.l: global CO₂ from cement (widely cited estimate)

deep.x: Why cement emits
About half the emissions come from the chemistry itself, not the fuel.
Reductions
Design matters
Optimising structures to use less material can cut embodied carbon substantially at no extra cost.
The greenest material is the one you don't need to use.

cards.title: Corrosion
cards.text: Steel rusts when exposed to oxygen and water, especially with salt. Protection includes paint, galvanising (zinc coating), stainless alloys and keeping concrete cover over rebar.

deep.x: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of metals by chemical reaction with their environment. Rusting steel is the most familiar form.
What drives rust
Salt accelerates corrosion, which is why coastal and road-salted structures suffer most.
Rebar corrosion
Rusting steel expands inside concrete, cracking it from within (spalling). Adequate concrete cover and good quality concrete protect rebar.
Cost
Corrosion costs are estimated at around 3% of global GDP each year.
Keep water and salt away from steel, and it lasts.

cards.title: Glass
cards.text: Glass is very strong in compression but brittle: a tiny scratch can start a crack. Tempered glass is heat-treated to be much stronger and shatters into small blunt pieces; laminated glass holds together.

deep.x: Glass is stiff and strong in compression but brittle. Tiny surface flaws can start cracks that spread instantly.
Laminated glass
Two or more sheets bonded with a plastic interlayer stay together when broken. Car windscreens and glass floors use it.
Why glass is "weak"
In theory, glass is extremely strong. In practice, microscopic scratches concentrate stress and start cracks.
Uses
Tempered glass can't be cut after treatment; it must be shaped first.

quiz.q: Why does reinforced concrete contain steel bars?
options: Concrete is weak in tension, so steel carries the tensile forces

quiz.q: Wood is strongest…
Which is the lightest per volume?
quiz.explain: Aluminium is about a third of steel's density.

lessons.title: Stress and strain
lessons.summary: How materials stretch, bend and break.

cards.title: Stress
example: 10 kN on a 100 mm² steel bar
cards.text: Stress is force divided by the area carrying it. The same force on a thinner bar creates more stress. Units: pascals (N/m²), usually megapascals (MPa).

deep.x: Stress is force divided by the area carrying it. It tells you how hard the material is working, regardless of size.
Units
Example

x: 10 kN on a 10 mm diameter steel rod

deep.x: Types of stress
Stress shows how hard each square millimetre is working.

cards.title: Strain
cards.text: Strain is how much a material stretches compared with its original length. It has no units and is usually tiny.

deep.x: Strain is the change in length divided by the original length. It's a ratio with no units, usually very small.
Example
Measuring strain
Strain gauges, thin foil patterns glued to a surface, change resistance as they stretch. They monitor bridges, aircraft and weighing scales.
Microstrain
Strain is stretch per unit length.

cards.title: Young's modulus
cards.text: Stiffness is measured by Young's modulus: stress divided by strain. Steel is about 200 GPa, aluminium about 70, wood about 10 along the grain.

deep.x: Young's modulus measures stiffness: how much stress is needed for a given strain in the elastic range.
What it means
Steel is about three times stiffer than aluminium. An aluminium part needs to be deeper or thicker to match a steel part's stiffness.
History
Named after English scientist Thomas Young, who described it in 1807, though similar ideas were explored earlier.
Hooke's law

items.m: Springs stretch in proportion to force

deep.x: Young's modulus is a material's stiffness, independent of shape.

cards.title: Elastic and plastic
cards.text: In the elastic range, a material springs back when unloaded. Past the yield point it deforms permanently (plastic). Engineers design structures to stay elastic in normal use.

deep.x: In the elastic range, materials spring back fully when unloaded. Beyond the yield point, they deform permanently.
Everyday examples
Design principle
Structures are designed to stay elastic under normal loads. Plastic behaviour provides a reserve in extreme events, like earthquakes.
Elastic means it returns; plastic means it remembers.

cards.title: The stress–strain curve
cards.text: Testing a steel bar in a machine draws a curve: a straight elastic line, a yield point, then plastic stretching up to the ultimate strength, and finally fracture.

deep.x: Tensile testing pulls a sample until it breaks, recording a stress-strain curve that reveals key properties.
Key values from the curve
Necking
After the ultimate strength, the bar narrows locally ("necks"), and the force needed drops until fracture.
Typical structural steel
One test reveals stiffness, strength and ductility.

cards.title: Ductile vs brittle
cards.text: Ductile materials (steel, copper) stretch a lot before breaking, giving warning. Brittle ones (glass, cast iron, concrete) snap suddenly. Ductility makes structures safer.

deep.x: Ductile materials stretch and bend significantly before breaking. Brittle materials fracture suddenly with little deformation.
Why ductility matters
A ductile structure bends and sags before collapsing, giving people time to escape and engineers warning signs.
Temperature effects
Some steels become brittle in extreme cold. The Liberty ships of World War II suffered brittle fractures in cold seas, prompting new research into steel toughness.
Earthquake design
Seismic codes require ductile detailing: steel reinforcement arranged so concrete members bend without sudden collapse.
Ductility is a material's way of warning you.

cards.title: Bending stress
cards.text: When a beam bends, stress is zero at the middle (neutral axis) and greatest at the top and bottom surfaces. That's why I-beams put material far from the middle.

deep.x: When a beam bends, stress varies across its depth: zero at the neutral axis, maximum at the top and bottom surfaces.
Stress distribution
Consequences

items: I-beams put material at top and bottom
Holes near the neutral axis do little harm

deep.x: Maximum moment

x: Simply supported beam, central load P, span L

deep.x: Bending works the surfaces hardest.

cards.title: Second moment of area
cards.text: A beam's resistance to bending depends hugely on its depth. For a rectangle, doubling the depth makes it eight times stiffer. That's why joists are placed on edge.

deep.x: The second moment of area (I) describes how a cross-section's shape resists bending. Depth matters enormously.
Depth vs width

v.unit: relative stiffness of a rectangular section

deep.x: Why joists stand on edge
Practical lessons

x: Deeper beams are much stiffer for the same material
Shelves sag less if they have a deep front lip
Ruler: easy to bend flat, very hard on edge

deep.x: Depth is cubed: double it and stiffness rises eightfold.

cards.title: Thermal expansion
cards.text: Materials grow when heated. A 100 m steel bridge can lengthen about 4 cm between winter and summer, so it has expansion joints. Rails, pipes and concrete slabs need room to move too.

deep.x: Materials expand when heated and contract when cooled. Structures must accommodate this movement.
Example
Coefficients
Solutions

items: Gaps in rails (or welded, stressed rails)
Movement joints in slabs and tiles

deep.x: Mixing materials
Steel and concrete expand at almost the same rate, one reason reinforced concrete works so well.
Leave room to grow: materials move with temperature.

cards.title: Stress concentrations

items.w: sharp internal corner
square window in a pressurised cabin

cards.text: Sharp corners, holes and notches concentrate stress, sometimes to three times the average. Rounded corners (fillets) spread it out. Aircraft windows are rounded for this reason.

deep.x: Holes, notches and sharp corners concentrate stress locally, sometimes to several times the average. Cracks start there.

items.w: Sharp internal corner in a loaded part

deep.x: Stress concentration factor
The Comet disasters

In 1954, two de Havilland Comet jet airliners broke up in flight. Investigations traced fatigue cracks to sharp corners of openings in the pressurised fuselage. Since then, aircraft openings and windows have rounded corners.
Design practice
Sharp corners are where cracks are born.

quiz.q: 20 kN on a 400 mm² bar gives a stress of…
Turning a plank on edge makes it much stiffer because…
options: Bending stiffness grows with depth cubed

quiz.q: Which material gives warning before breaking?

lessons.title: Friction
lessons.summary: The force that grips, slows and wears things down.

cards.title: What friction is
cards.text: Friction resists sliding between surfaces. At a microscopic level, even smooth surfaces are rough, and bumps catch and briefly bond.

deep.x: Friction resists sliding between surfaces. At the microscopic level, even polished surfaces are rough, touching only at tiny high points.
Classic laws

items.b: kinetic friction roughly independent of speed

deep.x: Leonardo first
Leonardo da Vinci studied friction around 1500, two centuries before Amontons, but his notes weren't published.
Energy
Friction turns motion into heat. Rub your hands together and feel it.
Friction is countless microscopic contacts resisting motion.

cards.title: Coefficient of friction
cards.text: Friction force is roughly the normal force (how hard surfaces press together) times a coefficient μ that depends on the materials.

deep.x: The friction force is roughly the normal force multiplied by a coefficient (μ) that depends on the two materials.
Example

x: 1,000 N box on wood floor, μ ≈ 0.4

deep.x: Variability
Coefficients vary with surface condition, moisture, temperature and contamination. Engineers use conservative values.
Friction depends on the pair of materials and how hard they press.

cards.title: Static vs kinetic
cards.text: It takes more force to start something sliding than to keep it going. Static friction is higher than kinetic (sliding) friction. That's why ABS keeps wheels from locking.

deep.x: It takes more force to start sliding than to keep sliding. Static friction is generally higher than kinetic friction.
ABS brakes
A rolling tyre uses static friction at the contact patch; a locked, sliding tyre uses lower kinetic friction and can't steer.
Stick-slip
Alternating sticking and slipping causes squeaky doors, creaking floors and violin sounds.
Once it starts sliding, it's easier to keep it sliding.

cards.title: Brakes
cards.text: Brakes turn motion into heat through friction between pads and discs. On a long descent, brakes can overheat and fade; using engine braking or EV regeneration helps.

deep.x: Brakes convert kinetic energy into heat through friction between pads and discs or drums.
Energy involved

x: All turned to heat in a stop

deep.x: Brake fade
On long descents, brakes overheat and friction drops. Using lower gears (engine braking) or EV regenerative braking prevents fade.
Brake types
Brake dust
Brake wear releases fine particles, a significant source of urban air pollution. EVs produce less because they brake mostly by regeneration.
Brakes turn speed into heat.

cards.title: Tyres and grip
cards.text: Tyres grip through friction and slight deformation of the rubber. On wet roads, tread grooves channel water away; without them, the tyre can aquaplane on a water film.

deep.x: Tyres grip the road through friction and the rubber's slight deformation into the road surface texture.
Aquaplaning
Tread depth
Stopping distances

v.unit: stopping distance from 80 km/h in wet, m (illustrative)

deep.x: Pressure
Under-inflated tyres overheat, wear unevenly, increase fuel use and reduce grip.
Tyres are the only contact between car and road: about four postcards' worth.

cards.title: Lubrication
cards.text: Oil and grease separate surfaces with a thin film, cutting friction and wear dramatically. Engines, bearings and gearboxes depend on it.

deep.x: Lubricants separate surfaces with a thin film, dramatically reducing friction and wear.
Lubrication regimes
Types
Engine oil
Engine oil lubricates, cools, cleans and protects against corrosion. Changing it at recommended intervals prevents expensive wear.
A film thinner than a hair separates metal from metal.

cards.title: Bearings
cards.text: Ball and roller bearings replace sliding with rolling, which has far lower friction. They're in wheels, motors, fans and hard drives.

deep.x: Bearings support rotating shafts with minimal friction. Rolling bearings replace sliding with rolling.
Types
Where they are
Failure signs
Rolling beats sliding by a factor of a hundred.

cards.title: Useful friction
cards.text: Without friction you couldn't walk, drive, hold a pen or keep a nut on a bolt. Engineers often add friction on purpose: clutch plates, belt drives, non-slip floors.

deep.x: Friction isn't just an enemy. Much of daily life depends on it, and engineers often add it on purpose.
Engineered friction
Friction in fasteners
Bolted joints hold mainly through friction between clamped surfaces, created by bolt tension. That's why correct torque matters.
Without friction
Imagine walking on perfectly frictionless ice: you couldn't start, stop or turn.
Friction holds the world together.

cards.title: Rolling resistance
cards.text: Even rolling tyres lose energy as the rubber flexes. Low-rolling-resistance tyres and correct pressure save fuel or EV range.

deep.x: Rolling tyres lose energy because rubber flexes and recovers with each rotation. This rolling resistance affects fuel use and EV range.
Why trains are efficient
Steel wheels on steel rails deform very little, giving rolling resistance about a tenth of car tyres.
Saving energy
EU tyre label
EU tyre labels rate rolling resistance (energy efficiency), wet grip and noise, helping buyers compare.
Pump up your tyres: it's free efficiency.

cards.title: Wear costs

items.l: of world energy used to overcome friction (estimate)

cards.text: Friction and wear are estimated to consume around a fifth of the world's energy and cause large losses through worn parts, according to tribology studies. Better lubricants and materials save a lot.

deep.x: Friction and wear consume a large share of the world's energy and cause huge losses through worn components.

items.l: world energy used to overcome friction (estimate)
the science of friction, wear and lubrication

deep.x: Where energy goes
Savings potential
Studies by tribologists such as Kenneth Holmberg and Ali Erdemir suggest new technologies could cut friction losses significantly over decades.
Solutions
Reducing friction is one of the quietest ways to save energy.

quiz.q: A 50 kg box (≈490 N) on a floor with μ = 0.4 needs about how much force to slide?
Why is it harder to start pushing a box than to keep it moving?
options: Static friction is higher than kinetic friction
quiz.explain: Starting needs to overcome static friction.

quiz.q: What do ball bearings do?
quiz.explain: Rolling resists far less than sliding.

lessons.title: Work, energy and power
lessons.summary: Lifting, moving and how fast it happens.

cards.title: Work
cards.text: Work is done when a force moves something: force times distance. Lift a 10 kg bag 1 m and you do about 98 J of work.

deep.x: In physics, work is done when a force moves something in the direction of the force. It's measured in joules.

items.m: distance moved in the force's direction

deep.x: Example
No movement, no work
Holding a heavy bag still does no physical work, even though your muscles tire. Your muscles use energy to stay tense, but nothing moves.
Everyday work
Work is force multiplied by distance moved.

cards.title: Potential energy
cards.text: Raising something stores energy that can be released when it falls. Hydroelectric dams use this with millions of tonnes of water.

deep.x: Raising an object against gravity stores gravitational potential energy, which can be released when it falls.
Example
Hydroelectric power
Pumped storage
Portugal's pumped-storage plants pump water uphill when electricity is cheap and release it when needed, storing energy as height.
Other forms

items: Raised weights in gravity storage systems

deep.x: Height is stored energy.

cards.title: Kinetic energy
example: 1,500 kg car at 50 km/h vs 100 km/h
cards.text: Moving objects carry energy that grows with the square of speed. Double the speed and the energy quadruples, which is why speed matters so much in crashes.

deep.x: Moving objects carry kinetic energy, which grows with the square of speed.
Speed matters most

v.unit: kinetic energy of a 1,500 kg car, kJ

deep.x: In crashes
Doubling speed quadruples the energy a crash must absorb. Going from 50 to 70 km/h nearly doubles crash energy.
Braking distance
Braking distance also rises with the square of speed, because brakes must remove all that energy.
Double the speed, four times the energy.

cards.title: Power
cards.text: Power is how fast work is done: joules per second, or watts. A strong cyclist sustains about 200–300 W; a car engine delivers tens to hundreds of kW.

deep.x: Power is the rate of doing work or using energy, measured in watts: joules per second.
Peak vs sustained
Climbing stairs
Power is how fast the work gets done.

cards.title: Horsepower
cards.text: James Watt defined horsepower to sell steam engines: about 746 W in the imperial version. The metric horsepower (cv in Portugal) is about 735 W.

deep.x: James Watt defined the horsepower in the 1780s to compare his steam engines with the draft horses they replaced.
Converting
Was it realistic?
Watt estimated a horse could sustain about 33,000 foot-pounds per minute. Real horses can produce more in short bursts but less over a full day.
Car specs in Portugal
Portuguese car advertisements often quote power in cv, while technical documents use kW. EU documents require kW.
One horsepower is about three-quarters of a kilowatt.

cards.title: Efficiency
cards.text: No machine converts all input energy into useful output; some becomes heat or noise. Efficiency is useful output divided by input.

deep.x: No machine converts all input energy into useful output. Efficiency is the useful output divided by the input.

items.m: The rest becomes heat, noise, vibration

deep.x: Where losses go
Chains of efficiency
Every conversion loses something; fewer conversions lose less.

cards.title: Energy is conserved

steps: Top of the hill: potential energy

cards.text: Energy changes form but the total stays the same. A falling roller coaster turns potential energy into kinetic energy, then back again, minus friction losses.

deep.x: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another. The total always stays the same.

steps: Friction slowly turns it to heat

deep.x: Roller coasters
A roller coaster's first hill is the tallest because no later hill can be higher: friction has already turned some energy into heat.
Forms of energy
Perpetual motion

items.w: A machine that runs forever with no energy input
items.r: Impossible: friction always turns some energy into heat

deep.x: Energy changes form but never disappears.

cards.title: Joules and kWh
cards.text: Engineers use joules; electricity bills use kWh. One kWh is 3.6 million joules, the energy of a 1 kW heater running for an hour.

deep.x: Engineers and scientists measure energy in joules; electricity bills use kilowatt-hours. Converting between them is simple.
Everyday energy
Food vs electricity
A human runs on roughly the energy of a 100 W bulb.
3.6 million joules make one kilowatt-hour.

cards.title: Energy in fuels
cards.text: A litre of petrol holds about 9 kWh of chemical energy, which is why liquid fuels were so hard to beat. Lithium batteries hold far less per kilo, but electric drivetrains use energy much more efficiently.

deep.x: Liquid fuels pack a lot of energy into a small volume, which is why they dominated transport for a century.
Why EVs still compete
Per litre
Hydrogen
Hydrogen has huge energy per kilo but very little per litre unless compressed or liquefied, making storage hard.
Fuel stores lots of energy; electric motors waste less of it.

cards.title: Springs
cards.text: A spring stores energy when stretched or compressed. Its force is proportional to how far it moves (Hooke's law), used in suspensions, scales and clocks.

deep.x: Springs store energy when stretched or compressed. Within their elastic range, force is proportional to deflection.

v.f: F = k × x; Energy = ½ × k × x²

deep.x: Uses
Example

x: Spring with k = 10,000 N/m compressed 5 cm

deep.x: Fatigue
Springs that flex millions of times can fail by fatigue. Valve springs in engines are designed for billions of cycles.
Robert Hooke published his law in 1678 as a Latin anagram, "ceiiinosssttuv", standing for "ut tensio, sic vis": as the extension, so the force.

quiz.q: Kinetic energy at 100 km/h compared with 50 km/h is…
Lifting 20 kg by 2 m does about how much work?
1 kWh equals…

lessons.title: Fluids and hydraulics
lessons.summary: Pressure, buoyancy and the power of liquids.

cards.title: Pressure
cards.text: Pressure is force spread over an area. A stiletto heel presses far harder on the floor than an elephant's foot, because the area is tiny.

deep.x: Pressure is force spread over an area. The same force concentrated on a small area produces huge pressure.
Heel vs elephant
Units
Applications
Spread force to reduce pressure; concentrate it to cut.

cards.title: Pressure in water
cards.text: Water pressure increases with depth, about 1 bar every 10 metres. Divers feel it in their ears; dams are thicker at the bottom for the same reason.

deep.x: Water pressure increases steadily with depth, because of the weight of water above.
Roughly 1 bar per 10 m
Dams
Dams are thicker at the bottom, where water pressure is greatest. Large concrete dams can be many times thicker at the base than at the crest.
Divers
Divers equalise ear pressure as they descend. Every 10 m adds about one atmosphere.
Water towers

steps: Taps below get pressure without pumps running

deep.x: Every 10 metres of water adds one bar.

cards.title: Atmospheric pressure
cards.text: Air above us presses down with about 1 bar (101 kPa) at sea level, roughly 10 tonnes on every square metre. We don't notice because it pushes equally from all sides.

deep.x: The weight of the air above us creates atmospheric pressure, about 1 bar at sea level.
Why we don't notice
Pressure acts equally in all directions, and our bodies contain fluids at the same pressure, so forces balance.
The Magdeburg hemispheres
In 1654, Otto von Guericke pumped the air out of two joined copper hemispheres. Teams of horses couldn't pull them apart: atmospheric pressure held them together.
With altitude
We live at the bottom of an ocean of air.

cards.title: Pascal's principle
cards.text: Pressure in a closed liquid spreads equally in all directions. Push a small piston and a big piston feels the same pressure over a larger area, giving a bigger force.

deep.x: Pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally throughout. A small force on a small piston creates a large force on a large piston.
Example

x: Small piston 1 cm², big piston 100 cm²

deep.x: The trade-off
The small piston must move 100 times farther than the large one rises. Energy is conserved.
History
Blaise Pascal described the principle in the 1650s. Joseph Bramah patented the hydraulic press in 1795.
Fluids are nearly incompressible

items: air in brake lines is dangerous

deep.x: Pressure travels; area multiplies force.

cards.title: Hydraulics everywhere
cards.text: Car brakes, excavators, lifts and presses use hydraulic fluid to multiply force and transmit it through flexible hoses.

deep.x: Hydraulic systems multiply and transmit force through fluid in hoses and cylinders. They're compact, powerful and controllable.
Car brakes
Why hydraulics
Brake fluid
Brake fluid absorbs moisture over time, lowering its boiling point. That's why it should be replaced every couple of years.
Hydraulics put enormous force at the end of a flexible hose.

cards.title: Buoyancy
cards.text: An object in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces (Archimedes). If that's more than its own weight, it floats. Steel ships float because their shape displaces a lot of water.

deep.x: Archimedes' principle: an object in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces.
Why steel ships float
A steel ship's hollow shape displaces a large volume of water, whose weight equals the ship's weight before the hull is fully submerged.
Density decides

items.b: floats in salt water more easily

deep.x: Submarines
Submarines flood or empty ballast tanks to change their average density, letting them dive or surface.
According to legend, Archimedes shouted "Eureka!" when he realised in his bath how to test whether a king's crown was pure gold.

cards.title: Flow in pipes
cards.text: Flow rate equals speed times pipe area. Squeeze a hose and the water speeds up. Narrow pipes need more pressure to push the same flow because of friction.

deep.x: The flow rate of a fluid is its speed multiplied by the pipe's cross-section. In a narrower section, the fluid speeds up.
Squeeze the hose
Friction losses
Friction losses rise steeply with speed, so undersized pipes waste pumping energy.
Home plumbing
Same flow through a smaller pipe means faster water and more friction.

cards.title: Bernoulli
cards.text: Where a fluid moves faster, its pressure drops. This helps explain carburettors, atomisers and part of how wings and sails create lift.

deep.x: Bernoulli's principle, published by Daniel Bernoulli in 1738, says that where a fluid flows faster, its pressure is lower (along a streamline).
Examples
Venturi tube

steps: Narrow throat: speed rises, pressure falls

deep.x: Lift and Bernoulli
Bernoulli's principle helps explain the pressure difference on wings, but popular "equal transit time" explanations are wrong. Lift is best understood as the wing deflecting air downward.
Faster flow, lower pressure.

cards.title: Siphons
cards.text: A siphon moves liquid up over a barrier and down to a lower point without a pump, as long as the outlet is below the source and the tube starts full.

deep.x: A siphon moves liquid from a higher container to a lower one, over a barrier, without a pump, once the tube is filled.
Limits

items.b: about 10 m for water at sea level

deep.x: Uses
How it works
Gravity pulling liquid down the longer leg, together with atmospheric pressure and the liquid's cohesion, keeps the flow going.
Fill the tube, keep the outlet low, and gravity does the pumping.

cards.title: Viscosity
cards.text: Viscosity is a fluid's thickness: honey is viscous, water isn't. Oil grades like 5W-30 describe how viscosity behaves when cold (5W) and hot (30).

deep.x: Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flow: its "thickness". Honey is highly viscous; water isn't.

v.unit: approx. viscosity, mPa·s at room temperature

deep.x: Temperature
Most liquids become thinner when hot and thicker when cold. Engine oil must flow when cold and still protect when hot.
Oil grades
Non-Newtonian fluids
Viscosity is how much a fluid resists flowing.

quiz.q: Roughly how much does pressure increase per 10 m of water depth?
A hydraulic jack with an area ratio of 20 turns 50 N into…
Why does a steel ship float?
options: Its shape displaces a weight of water greater than its own

lessons.title: How planes fly
lessons.summary: Lift, drag, thrust and weight.

cards.title: Four forces
cards.text: In steady flight, lift balances weight and thrust balances drag. To climb, lift exceeds weight; to speed up, thrust exceeds drag.

deep.x: In flight, four forces act on an aircraft: lift, weight, thrust and drag.
Steady flight
In level flight at constant speed, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag. The plane isn't "pushing harder" than in cruise; forces are balanced.
Manoeuvres
Weight changes
Airliners burn tens of tonnes of fuel on long flights, getting lighter and able to climb to higher, more efficient altitudes.
Steady flight is a balance of four forces.

cards.title: How wings make lift
cards.text: A wing is shaped and tilted (angle of attack) to deflect air downwards. Pushing air down pushes the wing up (Newton's third law), with lower pressure above the wing and higher below.

deep.x: A wing creates lift by deflecting air downward. By Newton's third law, pushing air down pushes the wing up.
Two views, one phenomenon
Both describe the same physics.
A myth

items.w: Air over the top must meet the air underneath at the trailing edge
items.r: Air over the top actually arrives sooner, equal transit time is false

deep.x: Angle of attack
Even a flat plate generates lift at an angle. The curved shape (camber) makes wings more efficient and gentler at stalling.
Wings fly by pushing air down.

cards.title: The lift equation

viz.f: L = ½ × ρ × v² × S × CL

cards.text: Lift grows with air density, wing area and the square of speed. That's why planes need long runways at hot, high airports where air is thin.

deep.x: Lift depends on air density, speed, wing area and a lift coefficient set by wing shape and angle of attack.

v.f: L = ½ × ρ × v² × S × CL

deep.x: Speed squared
Hot and high
Hot air and high altitudes mean thinner air. Planes need higher speeds and longer runways to take off from airports such as Mexico City or La Paz.
Weight limits
On hot days at high-altitude airports, airlines sometimes reduce passengers, cargo or fuel to take off safely.
Thin air demands more speed for the same lift.

cards.title: Stall
cards.text: Increase the angle of attack too much and the airflow separates from the upper surface. Lift collapses suddenly: a stall. Pilots train to recognise and recover from it.

deep.x: A stall occurs when the wing's angle of attack is too high. Airflow separates from the upper surface and lift drops sharply.
Stall isn't engine failure

items.w: "The engine stalled, so the plane fell"
items.r: An aerodynamic stall is about wing angle, not engines

deep.x: Recovery
Warnings
Aircraft have stall warning systems: horns, stick shakers and, in modern airliners, protections that limit angle of attack.
Air France 447
In 2009, Air France flight 447 crashed into the Atlantic after the crew failed to recognise and recover from a high-altitude stall, a tragedy that reshaped pilot training.
Stall depends on angle, not speed alone.

cards.title: Flaps and slats
cards.text: For take-off and landing, flaps and slats extend from the wing to increase its area and curvature, giving more lift at low speed.

deep.x: Flaps and slats change a wing's shape for slow flight, allowing take-off and landing at lower speeds.
How they help

items.b: extend from trailing edge, increase area and camber
extend from leading edge, delay stall
reduce lift and add drag after landing

deep.x: Landing speeds
Watch from the window
Next time you fly, watch the wing transform before landing: slats move forward, flaps slide back and down, and spoilers pop up on touchdown.
Flaps let a fast wing fly slowly.

cards.title: Drag
cards.text: Drag comes from friction with the air and from the pressure difference behind the object. It grows with the square of speed, so going faster costs a lot more fuel.

deep.x: Drag resists motion through air. It rises with the square of speed, so faster travel costs disproportionately more energy.

v.f: D = ½ × ρ × v² × S × CD

deep.x: Types of drag
Power needed
Power to overcome drag rises with the cube of speed: cycling at 30 km/h takes far more effort than at 20 km/h.
Winglets
Upturned wingtips reduce induced drag, saving several percent of fuel on airliners.
Speed costs: drag squares it, power cubes it.

cards.title: Jet engines

steps: Turbine and exhaust push the plane

cards.text: A turbofan sucks in air, compresses it, burns fuel in it and blasts the hot gas out the back. Most thrust in airliners comes from the big fan pushing air around the core.

deep.x: Modern airliners use turbofan engines: a large fan pushes most air around the engine core, providing most of the thrust efficiently.

steps: Some air to core: compressed, burned, expanded

deep.x: Bypass ratio
Why big fans
Accelerating a lot of air gently is more efficient than accelerating a little air violently. That's why modern engines have huge fans.
Temperatures
Turbine blades operate in gas hotter than their melting point, protected by cooling air channels and special coatings.
Most of a modern jet's thrust comes from its fan.

cards.title: Why airliners cruise high
cards.text: At about 10–12 km altitude, the air is thin, so drag is much lower and jet engines are more efficient. Cabins are pressurised to the equivalent of about 2,000 m.

deep.x: At 10–12 km altitude, thin air reduces drag, and jet engines run efficiently. Most weather is also below.
Cabin pressure
Cabins are pressurised to the equivalent of about 1,800–2,400 m altitude. Newer composite aircraft like the Boeing 787 use lower cabin altitudes and higher humidity for comfort.
Above the weather

items: Jet streams can speed up eastbound flights

deep.x: Contrails
Contrails form when hot, humid exhaust meets cold air and water freezes into ice crystals. Their climate effect is an active research area.
High altitude means thin air, low drag and efficient engines.

cards.title: Control surfaces
cards.text: Ailerons on the wings roll the plane, the elevator on the tail pitches it up and down, and the rudder yaws it left and right.

deep.x: Pilots control an aircraft's attitude around three axes using movable surfaces.

items.b: on wings, roll left and right
on tail, pitch nose up and down
on fin, yaw nose left and right

deep.x: Coordinated turns
Fly-by-wire
Modern airliners use fly-by-wire: pilot inputs go to computers, which move control surfaces and protect against dangerous manoeuvres.
Trim
Trim tabs adjust surfaces so the plane flies steadily without constant pilot force.
Roll, pitch and yaw: three axes, three controls.

cards.title: Drones
cards.text: Multirotor drones have no wings; they create lift by spinning propellers. They steer by speeding up some motors and slowing others, with a flight controller adjusting hundreds of times a second.

deep.x: Multirotor drones fly without wings, using spinning propellers for lift and changing their speeds to steer.
Control by speed differences
Sensors
Efficiency
Rules
EU drone rules require registration of operators for most drones with cameras, and limit flights near people and airports.
Drones steer by changing motor speeds hundreds of times a second.

quiz.q: What happens in a stall?
options: The wing's airflow separates and lift drops sharply
quiz.explain: Too high an angle of attack.

quiz.q: Doubling speed changes drag by a factor of about…
Which control surface rolls the plane?
quiz.explain: Ailerons move in opposite directions on each wing.

lessons.title: Bridges
lessons.summary: Beam, arch, suspension and cable-stayed.

cards.title: The main bridge types
cards.text: Bridges handle loads differently: beams bend, arches compress, suspension cables pull, and cable-stayed towers hold the deck with straight cables.

deep.x: Bridge types differ in how they carry loads to the ground: by bending, compression or tension.
Typical spans
Choosing
Record holders
The world's longest suspension span, the 1915 Çanakkale Bridge in Turkey (2022), spans just over 2 km.
Each bridge type uses a different force to cross the gap.

cards.title: Beam bridges
cards.text: The simplest bridge: a beam on supports. Cheap and quick for short spans, but deep beams are needed as the span grows, so they're often continuous over many piers.

deep.x: A beam bridge is a horizontal beam resting on supports. It's the simplest and most common bridge type.
Limits
As spans grow, beams must get much deeper to stay stiff, adding weight. Beyond a few hundred metres, other types are more efficient.
Viaducts
Long viaducts are often chains of beam spans on many piers, like motorway viaducts across valleys.
Construction
Beam bridges are simple, cheap and everywhere.

cards.title: Arch bridges
cards.text: Arches carry loads in compression to strong abutments. Stone arches have lasted for 2,000 years. Porto's Dom Luís I bridge (1886) is a double-deck iron arch over the Douro.

deep.x: Arch bridges carry loads in compression to strong abutments. Stone arches have lasted for millennia.
Porto's arches

items.b: 1877, iron railway arch by Eiffel's company
1886, double-deck iron arch by Théophile Seyrig

deep.x: Arrábida
When it opened in 1963, Edgar Cardoso's Arrábida Bridge had the longest reinforced concrete arch span in the world, about 270 m.
Roman legacy
The Pont du Gard aqueduct in France and Portugal's Roman bridges, like the one at Chaves, still stand after nearly 2,000 years.
Porto's bridges are a museum of arch engineering.

cards.title: Suspension bridges
cards.text: Main cables hang from tall towers and are anchored at each end; vertical hangers hold the deck. They achieve the longest spans. Lisbon's 25 de Abril bridge (1966) is one.

deep.x: Suspension bridges hang their decks from cables draped over towers and anchored at both ends. They achieve the longest spans.

steps: Anchorages in rock or massive blocks

deep.x: Lisbon's 25 de Abril Bridge
When it opened, it had the longest suspension span outside the United States.
Cable construction
Main cables are spun from thousands of parallel steel wires, compacted and wrapped. Each wire is only about 5 mm thick.
Flexibility
Suspension bridges move noticeably in wind and under traffic; this is normal and designed for.
Suspension bridges hang the road from cables in tension.

cards.title: Cable-stayed bridges
cards.text: Straight cables run directly from towers to the deck in a fan or harp pattern. Efficient for medium-long spans and quick to build. Lisbon's Vasco da Gama bridge has a cable-stayed main span.

deep.x: Cable-stayed bridges support the deck with straight cables running directly from towers. They're efficient for medium to long spans.
Patterns
Vasco da Gama Bridge
It was among the longest bridges in Europe when built, crossing the Tagus estuary.
Popularity
Cable-stayed bridges have become the most popular choice for spans between about 200 and 1,000 m.
Straight cables, simple towers, efficient spans.

cards.title: Portuguese bridges
cards.text: Portugal has some remarkable bridges, including several by Gustave Eiffel's company and Edgar Cardoso.

deep.x: Portugal has a rich bridge heritage, from Roman stone to record-breaking modern spans.
Edgar Cardoso
Engineer Edgar Cardoso (1913–2000) designed many notable Portuguese bridges, including the Arrábida and Edgar Cardoso bridges, and pioneered structural model testing.
Eiffel's connection
Infante D. Henrique Bridge
Porto's Infante D. Henrique Bridge (2003), designed by Adão da Fonseca, has a remarkably shallow concrete arch spanning about 280 m beneath a stiff deck.
Porto alone shows 150 years of bridge history across one river.

cards.title: Wind and Tacoma Narrows
cards.text: In 1940 the Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge in the US twisted itself apart in a moderate wind, due to aerodynamic instability. Since then, decks are wind-tunnel tested and shaped to avoid it.

deep.x: In November 1940, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State twisted itself apart in a wind of about 64 km/h, just months after opening.
Flutter, not simple resonance
The failure is often attributed to resonance, but engineers now describe it as aeroelastic flutter: the deck's motion changed the airflow in a way that kept adding energy.
Lessons
Filmed
The collapse was filmed and became one of the most famous engineering films ever, still used in teaching.
Bridges must be designed for how wind moves them, not just how hard it blows.

cards.title: Expansion joints
cards.text: Bridges grow and shrink with temperature. Expansion joints (the metal teeth you drive over) and sliding bearings let them move without cracking.

deep.x: Bridges expand and contract with temperature, and move under traffic and wind. Expansion joints and bearings allow this movement safely.
How much movement
Bearings
Maintenance
Joints suffer from traffic impact, debris and water. Damaged joints let water reach bearings and steel, causing corrosion.
The clatter as you drive over a joint is the bridge breathing.

cards.title: Foundations in rivers

steps: Flood water speeds up around pier

cards.text: Piers in rivers must resist scour: fast water digging away the riverbed around them. Many bridge failures come from scour during floods, not from the structure itself.

deep.x: Bridge piers in rivers must resist scour: fast-flowing water digging away the riverbed around foundations.
Entre-os-Rios

On 4 March 2001, the Hintze Ribeiro Bridge over the Douro at Entre-os-Rios collapsed during floods, killing 59 people. Scour around a pier, aggravated by sand extraction from the river, was identified as a key factor.
Protection
After the disaster
The tragedy led to major changes in Portuguese bridge inspection and management.
Many bridges fall because of what happens under the water.

cards.title: Inspection and maintenance
cards.text: Bridges are inspected regularly for cracks, corrosion, bearing wear and scour. Sensors increasingly monitor strain, vibration and movement in real time.

deep.x: Bridges need regular inspection and maintenance throughout their lives, often 100 years or more.
Inspection levels
Structural health monitoring
Genoa 2018
The collapse of Genoa's Morandi Bridge in August 2018, killing 43 people, intensified attention on ageing bridges and maintenance across Europe.
Bridges last a century only with a century of care.

quiz.q: Which bridge type carries loads mainly in compression?
Lisbon's 25 de Abril bridge is a…
What destroyed the Tacoma Narrows bridge in 1940?

lessons.title: Buildings and foundations
lessons.summary: From the ground up.

cards.title: Why foundations?
cards.text: Foundations spread a building's weight onto soil that can carry it without sinking unevenly. The weaker the soil, the bigger or deeper the foundations.

deep.x: Foundations transfer a building's loads safely to the ground, spreading them so the soil isn't overloaded and the building doesn't settle unevenly.
Soil strength
Site investigation
Design choice
The weaker the soil, the larger or deeper the foundations must be, sometimes reaching down tens of metres to firm layers.
A building is only as good as the ground it stands on.

cards.title: Shallow foundations
cards.text: Strip and pad footings, or a raft slab, work where firm soil or rock is near the surface. They're common for houses.

deep.x: Shallow foundations sit near the surface where good soil or rock is close. They're common for houses and low buildings.
Frost and moisture
Foundations must go below the depth affected by seasonal drying, frost or tree roots. In Portugal frost is rarely an issue, but clay shrinkage can be.
Raft foundations
On good ground, simple footings do the job.

cards.title: Deep foundations
cards.text: On soft ground, piles are driven or drilled down to firmer layers, carrying loads by end bearing and friction along their sides. Lisbon's Baixa was rebuilt after 1755 on wooden piles.

deep.x: Where surface soils are weak, piles carry loads down to stronger layers or develop resistance through friction along their length.

items: rest on rock or dense layers
rely on soil grip along their sides

deep.x: Pile types
Lisbon's Baixa
After the 1755 earthquake, the Baixa Pombalina was rebuilt on reclaimed, waterlogged ground using pine piles. Kept below the water table, wood resists rot for centuries.
Groundwater risk

items.w: Lowering the water table near old wooden piles
items.r: Monitor and protect: exposed piles can rot

deep.x: Piles reach past weak ground to something solid.

cards.title: Settlement

items.w: one corner on soft fill
cracks widening

cards.text: All buildings settle a little. Problems come from differential settlement, when one part sinks more than another, cracking walls and jamming doors.

deep.x: All buildings settle slightly as the soil compresses. Problems arise when settlement is uneven.

items.w: Some settlement means failure
items.r: Uniform settlement is normal, differential settlement causes damage

deep.x: Signs of differential settlement

items: Diagonal cracks near doors and windows

deep.x: Causes

items.b: soft and firm areas under one building

deep.x: The Leaning Tower of Pisa
Even settlement is fine; uneven settlement cracks walls.

cards.title: Walls and frames
cards.text: Traditional buildings have load-bearing walls of stone or brick. Modern ones use frames of concrete or steel columns and beams, with walls just filling the gaps.

deep.x: Buildings carry loads either through load-bearing walls or through frames of columns and beams.

items: concrete or steel columns and beams

deep.x: Traditional Portuguese buildings
Many older Portuguese buildings have thick stone or brick walls with timber floors. Later ones, from the mid-20th century, use reinforced concrete frames.
Renovation caution

items.w: Knocking through walls in old buildings
items.r: Check first: walls may carry the floors above

deep.x: Frame advantages
Know whether walls hold up the building or just divide rooms.

cards.title: The Pombaline cage
cards.text: After the 1755 earthquake, Lisbon was rebuilt with the "gaiola pombalina": a timber lattice of diagonal braces inside masonry walls, one of the first earthquake-resistant building systems in Europe.

deep.x: After the 1755 earthquake destroyed much of Lisbon, the city was rebuilt with an innovative earthquake-resistant system: the "gaiola pombalina".

steps: Timber frame of uprights and diagonals

deep.x: Who built it
The reconstruction under the Marquis of Pombal was led by engineers and architects including Manuel da Maia, Eugénio dos Santos and Carlos Mardel.
The marching test
According to historical accounts, troops marched around a model of the timber cage to simulate an earthquake and test its resistance.
Legacy
The Pombaline Baixa is often cited as one of the first examples of large-scale earthquake-resistant urban construction in the world.

cards.title: Earthquake design
cards.text: Seismic codes require buildings to sway without collapsing: ductile connections, bracing, shear walls, regular shapes. Some use base isolators that let the ground move beneath them.

deep.x: Seismic design aims to let buildings sway and deform without collapsing, protecting lives even in strong earthquakes.
Principles

items.b: beams yield first, columns stay standing

deep.x: Base isolation

steps: Rubber and steel bearings under building

deep.x: Portugal
Portugal applies the European seismic code (Eurocode 8). Many older buildings in Lisbon predate modern codes, making seismic retrofitting a priority.
Buildings can't stop earthquakes; they can survive them.

cards.title: Wind on tall buildings
cards.text: Wind pushes on tall buildings and makes them sway. Engineers stiffen them with cores and outriggers, and some skyscrapers use giant tuned mass dampers to cancel motion.

deep.x: Wind loads grow rapidly with height and can make tall buildings sway uncomfortably. Engineers stiffen and dampen them.
Solutions

items.b: concrete shafts for lifts and stairs

deep.x: Taipei 101
Taipei 101 has a 660-tonne steel ball suspended near its top as a tuned mass damper, visible to visitors.
Comfort
People feel sway long before it's dangerous. Designers limit accelerations to avoid motion sickness in occupants.
Tall buildings are designed to sway safely, and then dampened so you don't notice.

cards.title: Moisture and damp
cards.text: Water is the enemy of buildings: rising damp, leaks and condensation cause rot, mould and corrosion. Damp-proof courses, good roofs, gutters and ventilation keep it out.

deep.x: Water is one of the biggest threats to buildings, causing rot, mould, corrosion and damage to finishes.
Types of damp

items.b: moist indoor air on cold surfaces

deep.x: Portugal's challenge
Many Portuguese homes suffer condensation and mould in winter, because of poor insulation, cold surfaces and limited heating and ventilation.
Solutions
Keep water out, let moisture out.

cards.title: Burj Khalifa
cards.text: The world's tallest building, in Dubai, is 828 m high. Its Y-shaped plan and setbacks confuse the wind, and its foundations include 192 piles about 50 m long.

deep.x: Dubai's Burj Khalifa, completed in 2010, is the world's tallest building at 828 m.
Confusing the wind
The Y-shaped plan and spiralling setbacks change the building's shape with height, so wind vortices can't organise into a strong rhythm.
Structure
Records
What's next
Saudi Arabia's Jeddah Tower, under construction, aims to be the first building over 1 km tall.
Shape, not just strength, keeps the tallest tower standing.

quiz.q: What is differential settlement?
options: One part of a building sinking more than another

quiz.q: What was the gaiola pombalina?
options: A timber lattice inside walls for earthquake resistance

quiz.q: When are piles used?
options: On solid rock near the surface
On soft ground, to reach firmer layers
quiz.explain: They transfer loads to deeper strata.

lessons.title: Engines
lessons.summary: How petrol and diesel engines turn fuel into motion.

cards.title: The four-stroke cycle
cards.text: Most car engines repeat four strokes: suck in air and fuel, squeeze it, ignite it so it pushes the piston, and push out the exhaust. "Suck, squeeze, bang, blow."

deep.x: Most car engines run on the four-stroke cycle patented by Nikolaus Otto's company in 1876. Each cylinder repeats four piston strokes over two crankshaft turns.

steps: Power: spark ignites, piston pushed down

deep.x: "Suck, squeeze, bang, blow"

items.b: valves open, air and fuel drawn in
valves closed, pressure and temperature rise

deep.x: Only one stroke makes power
Three of the four strokes absorb energy. Multiple cylinders firing in sequence and a heavy flywheel keep rotation smooth.
Two-stroke engines
Four strokes, two turns, one bang per cylinder.

cards.title: Crankshaft
cards.text: Pistons move up and down; the crankshaft turns that into rotation, like legs pushing bicycle pedals. A flywheel smooths out the pulses.

deep.x: The crankshaft converts the pistons' up-and-down motion into rotation, just as your legs turn bicycle pedals.
Engine layouts

items.b: cylinders in a row, most small cars
two banks in a V, compact for more cylinders

deep.x: Balance
Engines are balanced to reduce vibration. Some four-cylinder engines add balance shafts spinning at twice crank speed.
Camshaft
The camshaft, driven by the crankshaft via a belt or chain, opens and closes the valves in time with the pistons.
The crankshaft turns pushes into spin.

cards.title: Petrol vs diesel
cards.text: Petrol engines use a spark to ignite the mixture. Diesels compress air so much that it gets hot enough to ignite fuel injected into it. Diesels are more efficient but heavier and produce more NOx and particles.

deep.x: Petrol and diesel engines differ in how they ignite fuel. That difference drives their efficiency, sound and emissions.
Efficiency
Dieselgate
In 2015, Volkswagen was found to have used software that detected emissions tests and reduced NOx only during testing. The scandal accelerated Europe's shift away from diesel cars.
Where diesel still dominates
Petrol uses sparks; diesel uses squeeze.

cards.title: Compression ratio
cards.text: Higher compression extracts more energy from the fuel. Petrol engines run about 10:1, diesels about 15–20:1. Too high in a petrol engine causes knocking.

deep.x: The compression ratio compares cylinder volume with the piston at the bottom and at the top. Higher compression extracts more energy from fuel.
Knock
Octane
Higher-octane petrol (98 vs 95) resists knock better, letting high-compression engines run safely. It doesn't add energy to normal engines.
Diesels need it
Diesels rely on high compression to heat air enough (over 500 °C) to ignite injected fuel.
Squeeze harder, extract more, until knock stops you.

cards.title: Turbochargers
cards.text: A turbo uses exhaust gas to spin a turbine that compresses intake air, forcing more air and fuel into the cylinders. Small engines can produce big power.

deep.x: A turbocharger uses exhaust energy to drive a compressor that forces extra air into the engine, allowing small engines to make big power.

steps: More air and fuel per cycle

deep.x: Downsizing
Turbo lag
Turbos need exhaust flow to spin up, so there's a delay after pressing the accelerator. Smaller turbos, twin turbos and electric assistance reduce lag.
Speed
Turbo shafts spin extremely fast, often over 100,000 rpm, and need good oil lubrication.
Turbos recycle exhaust energy into extra air.

cards.title: Torque and power
cards.text: Torque is the twisting force; power is torque times rotational speed. Diesels deliver strong torque at low rpm; petrol engines often make peak power at high rpm.

deep.x: Torque is twisting force; power is torque multiplied by rotational speed. Both matter, in different ways.
Example
What you feel

items.b: pull from low speed, towing, overtaking without changing gear
top speed, sustained acceleration at high revs

deep.x: Torque curves
EVs
Electric motors give maximum torque from zero rpm, which is why EVs feel so quick from standstill.
Torque pushes; power is how fast it keeps pushing.

cards.title: Gearboxes

items: keeps engine in its sweet spot

cards.text: Engines work best in a narrow speed range. Gears let the engine stay in that range whether the car is crawling or cruising. EV motors spin so widely they usually need just one gear.

deep.x: Combustion engines work efficiently only within a limited speed range. Gearboxes let the engine stay there whatever the road speed.
Gear ratios

items.b: low engine rpm at motorway speed

deep.x: Modern automatics
Many modern automatics have 8–10 gears, keeping engines near their most efficient speed.
EVs need one gear
Electric motors work efficiently from zero to over 15,000 rpm, so most EVs use a single reduction gear.
Gearboxes keep engines in their comfort zone.

cards.title: Cooling
cards.text: About a third of a fuel's energy leaves as heat through the cooling system, and another third through the exhaust. The radiator, coolant and thermostat keep the engine at its ideal temperature.

deep.x: Only around a third of fuel energy becomes useful work. The rest leaves as heat, through the cooling system and the exhaust.
The cooling system
Why not run cold?
Engines run most efficiently and cleanly at around 90 °C. The thermostat keeps coolant from the radiator until the engine warms up.
Overheating
Most of a fuel's energy heats the world, not the wheels.

cards.title: Emissions control
cards.text: Catalytic converters turn carbon monoxide, unburnt fuel and NOx into less harmful gases. Diesel particulate filters trap soot; AdBlue reduces NOx in diesels.

deep.x: Modern engines use several technologies to reduce harmful emissions.

items.b: CO, unburnt fuel and NOx into CO₂, water and nitrogen
recirculates exhaust to lower combustion temperature

deep.x: Euro standards
Catalysts need heat
Catalytic converters work only when hot. Most emissions on short trips happen in the first minutes after a cold start.
Real-world testing
After Dieselgate, the EU introduced Real Driving Emissions (RDE) tests on public roads.
Catalysts clean exhaust only once they're hot.

cards.title: Hybrids
cards.text: Hybrids pair a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery, recovering braking energy and helping the engine work efficiently. Plug-in hybrids can drive tens of kilometres on electricity alone.

deep.x: Hybrids combine a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery, recovering braking energy and helping the engine run efficiently.
Types
History
The Toyota Prius, launched in 1997, was the first mass-produced hybrid car.
Real-world plug-in use
Studies found plug-in hybrids often emit much more than official figures, because owners charge them less than assumed.
Plug-in hybrids save fuel only when plugged in.

quiz.q: What ignites the fuel in a diesel engine?
What does a turbocharger use to compress intake air?
Roughly what share of fuel energy becomes useful work in a petrol car engine?
quiz.explain: The rest is lost as heat.

lessons.title: Engineering an electric car
lessons.summary: Battery, motor, inverter and thermal management.

cards.title: The drivetrain
cards.text: An EV has far fewer moving parts than a combustion car: a battery pack, an inverter that turns DC into three-phase AC, an electric motor and a single-speed reduction gear.

deep.x: An electric car has far fewer moving parts than a combustion car. Its drivetrain is simple: battery, inverter, motor and gear.
Parts count
Motor placement

items.b: rear-wheel drive, common in performance EVs

deep.x: Efficiency
From battery to wheels, EV drivetrains typically convert 85–90% of energy into motion.
Fewer parts, less to go wrong.

cards.title: The skateboard platform
cards.text: Most EVs mount the battery flat under the floor between the axles. That lowers the centre of gravity, frees cabin space and stiffens the body.

deep.x: Most dedicated EV platforms place the battery flat under the floor between the axles, like a skateboard.
Handling
A low, central battery gives EVs a low centre of gravity, reducing body roll and rollover risk.
Space
With no engine or transmission tunnel, EVs often have flat floors and extra storage front and rear.
Structural packs

items: battery forms part of the floor structure

deep.x: The battery is the floor.

cards.title: Inverters
cards.text: The inverter switches the battery's DC on and off thousands of times a second with silicon or silicon-carbide transistors to create AC at whatever frequency the motor needs. Silicon carbide cuts losses, especially in 800 V cars.

deep.x: The inverter converts battery DC into three-phase AC at the frequency and voltage the motor needs, controlling speed and torque.

steps: Transistors switch thousands of times a second

deep.x: Silicon carbide
Tesla's Model 3 was among the first mass-market cars to use silicon carbide inverters.
Regeneration
The inverter also works in reverse during regenerative braking, converting motor AC into DC to charge the battery.
The inverter is the EV's conductor, directing every watt.

cards.title: Thermal management
cards.text: Batteries like about 20–40 °C. Liquid cooling plates, heat pumps and pre-conditioning keep them there for fast charging and long life, and reuse waste heat to warm the cabin.

deep.x: Batteries perform and last best within a comfortable temperature range. EVs actively heat and cool them.
Systems
Pre-conditioning

steps: Car warms battery on the way

deep.x: Cabin heating
Heat pumps can heat the cabin using two to three times less energy than resistive heaters, extending winter range.
Warm batteries charge fast; hot batteries age fast.

cards.title: Efficiency in kWh/100 km
cards.text: EV consumption is measured in kWh per 100 km. A compact car may use 14–16; a large SUV 20–24. Speed, cold and wind raise it a lot.

deep.x: EV consumption is measured in kWh per 100 km, the equivalent of litres per 100 km for combustion cars.
What raises it
Cost comparison
Speed matters
Motorway speed is the biggest range thief.

cards.title: Why range drops in winter

items: Battery chemistry slows in the cold

cards.text: Cold batteries have higher internal resistance, and heating the cabin takes energy. Range can fall by 20–30% in freezing weather; heat pumps reduce the loss.

deep.x: EVs lose range in cold weather because batteries are less efficient and heating the cabin takes energy.
How much
Reducing the loss
In Portugal
Portugal's mild winters mean range losses are usually modest compared with northern Europe.
Heat the people, not the whole cabin.

cards.title: Aerodynamics
cards.text: At motorway speeds, most energy goes into pushing air. EVs have smooth underbodies, flush handles and low drag coefficients (Cd around 0.2–0.3).

deep.x: At motorway speeds, overcoming air resistance uses most of an EV's energy. Every reduction in drag adds range.
Design features
Frontal area matters too

v.f: Drag force ∝ Cd × frontal area × speed²

deep.x: Small changes add up
A roof box can increase consumption by 10–25% at motorway speeds.
At 120 km/h, an EV spends most of its energy pushing air.

cards.title: Regenerative braking
cards.text: The motor acts as a generator when slowing down, recovering part of the energy. Friction brakes are still there for hard stops and are used less, so they last much longer.

deep.x: When slowing down, the motor acts as a generator, recovering part of the car's kinetic energy into the battery.
Blending
Modern EVs blend regenerative and friction braking automatically, using regeneration first and friction brakes when needed.
Brake life

items.b: often last much longer than in combustion cars
discs can rust from lack of use

deep.x: Efficiency
Regeneration recovers a meaningful share of energy in city driving, but each conversion loses some: it's better to coast than brake and regenerate.
The best braking is no braking; the second best is regeneration.

cards.title: Fewer parts, less maintenance

items: tyres, brake fluid, cabin filter, coolant

cards.text: No oil changes, spark plugs, clutch, exhaust or timing belt. Maintenance mostly involves tyres, brakes fluid, cabin filters and coolant.

deep.x: EVs need much less routine maintenance than combustion cars.
Tyres
EVs are heavy and torquey, so tyres may wear faster. Rotating them regularly and keeping correct pressures helps.
Running costs
Still check
EVs swap oil changes for tyre checks.

cards.title: Battery warranties
cards.text: Most manufacturers guarantee batteries for about 8 years or 160,000 km, typically to at least 70% capacity. Real-world data shows most packs degrade slowly.

deep.x: Most EV manufacturers guarantee their batteries for about 8 years or 160,000 km, typically to at least 70% of original capacity.
Real-world degradation
Data from large fleets suggest most EV batteries lose capacity slowly, often keeping around 90% after 100,000–200,000 km, with the biggest drop in the first years.
Protecting the battery

items: Limit frequent fast charging in heat

deep.x: EU battery rules
New EU battery regulations require battery passports and more information on health and durability, making used EV purchases more transparent.
EV batteries usually outlast expectations, and warranties cover the rest.

quiz.q: Which part converts the battery's DC into AC for the motor?
Why do EVs lose range in winter?
options: Cold batteries are less efficient and heating uses energy
quiz.explain: Both chemistry and cabin heating matter.
